alignment.note: The Syriac ܘܢܦܩܘ conflates the conjunction and verb into one prefixed form, so its index is shared with the preceding conjunction group; the action 'went out' (ἐξῆλθον / exierunt) agrees across all three.
The second conjunction 'and' (καὶ / et) is again fused in Syriac into ܘܫܪܝܘ ('and they began'), sharing the index with the following verb.
Greek ἤρξαντο and Latin cœperunt express the ingressive 'began' periphrasis; Syriac ܫܪܝܘ (root sh-r-y) carries the same inceptive sense within the fused form ܘܫܪܝܘ.

Greek συζητεῖν ('to dispute, debate') and Latin conquirere convey contentious questioning, whereas Syriac ܠܡܒܥܐ (root b-ʿ-a, 'to seek/inquire') is a milder lexical choice emphasising the act of requesting rather than disputation.
Greek encodes the comitative sense in the dative αὐτῷ; Latin renders it analytically with the preposition cum + eo; Syriac uses ܥܡܗ ('with him'). All are semantically equivalent.

Greek and Latin use a present participle (ζητοῦντες / quærentes, 'seeking'); Syriac employs a periphrastic construction ܫܐܠܝܢ ܗܘܘ (active participle + enclitic ܗܘܘ) expressing durative past action, a characteristic Syriac substitute for the participial circumstantial clause.

Greek παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ and Latin ab illo both render the prepositional 'from him' explicitly; Syriac contracts this to the dative-marking ܠܗ ('of/from him') governed by the verb of asking, omitting a separate ablative preposition.

All three read 'a sign from heaven'; the Greek articular genitive (ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ) and Latin de cælo correspond to Syriac ܡܢ ܫܡܝܐ, the Syriac noun being the formally plural ܫܡܝܐ used as a singular per Semitic idiom.

Greek πειράζοντες and Latin tentantes use a bare circumstantial participle ('testing'); Syriac introduces the subordinator ܟܕ ('while') + participle ܡܢܣܝܢ, making the temporal-circumstantial relation explicit where Greek and Latin leave it implicit.
